cards.text: The poet is still grieving over Zion, another name for Jerusalem. He opens this poem with one heavy word: "How." And the first thing he points to is the gold.

cards.question: The poet looks at Zion's pure gold. What has happened to it?

cards.text: The gems of the temple lie scattered on every street corner, and the precious sons of Zion, once worth their weight in pure gold, are now esteemed as jars of clay. I lost my shine in the back of a junk drawer and thought THAT was rough, friend, but this is a whole city.

cards.question: Zion's sons went from pure gold to ordinary clay jars. What is the poet saying about how they're seen now?

answers.text: They are seen as cheap and common
They are seen as strong and useful
They are seen as dangerous and wild

cards.text: Then the poet says even jackals nurse their young.

cards.question: Even jackals nurse their young. But the poet says the daughter of his people has become ___, like an ostrich in the wilderness.

cards.text: The nursing infant is so thirsty his tongue clings to the roof of his mouth.

cards.question: When the little children in Zion beg for bread, someone gives them some.

cards.text: Those who once ate delicacies are destitute in the streets, and those brought up in crimson huddle in ash heaps.

cards.question: People who once ate delicacies and were brought up in crimson now huddle in ash heaps. What is the poet showing?

answers.text: The poor have finally been fed
The people have moved to the country

cards.text: Then the poet brings up Sodom, the city the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on (Genesis 19:24). Sodom was overthrown in an instant, without a hand turned to help her.

cards.question: The poet says the punishment of the daughter of his people is greater than Sodom's.

cards.text: Now the poet remembers the city's dignitaries. They were brighter than snow, whiter than milk, more ruddy than rubies.

cards.question: Zion's dignitaries were once brighter than snow. What does the poet say their appearance is like now?
People still recognize Zion's dignitaries when they see them in the streets.

cards.text: Their skin has shriveled on their bones. It's as dry as a stick.

cards.question: The poet says some people waste away, pierced with pain, because the fields lack produce. Who does he say are better off than those who die of hunger?

answers.text: Those who hid in the hills

cards.text: This next part is heavy, friend. The poet says, "The hands of compassionate women have cooked their own children, who became their food in the destruction of the daughter of my people."
Then the poet says the LORD has exhausted His wrath. He has poured out His fierce anger.

cards.question: The poet says the LORD kindled a fire in Zion that consumed her ___.

cards.text: Now the poet steps back and looks at the whole world. The kings of the earth did not believe, and neither did any people of the world, that an enemy or a foe could enter the gates of Jerusalem.

cards.question: But the enemy got in. The poet says it was for the sins of those who shed the blood of the righteous in Jerusalem. Who were they?

cards.text: Those prophets and priests wandered blind in the streets, defiled by that blood. No one dared to touch their garments.

cards.question: When the defiled prophets and priests come near, men shout at them, "Go away! ___!"
When the prophets and priests flee and wander among the nations, they're welcomed to stay.

cards.text: The poet says the presence of the LORD has scattered them. He regards them no more.

cards.question: The poet says Zion's elders find no favor. How does he say her priests are treated now?

answers.text: They are praised for their service
They are welcomed by the nations

cards.text: Then the poet says their eyes were failing as they watched from their towers for a nation to help. I know that look, friend: back when I was stuck in that junk drawer, every rattle had me staring at the crack of light like it owed me money.

cards.question: The nation the people watched for from their towers was able to save them.

cards.text: And the enemy stalked their every step, so they couldn't even walk in their own streets. The poet says their end had come.

cards.question: The poet says the ones chasing his people were swifter than the eagles in the sky. What does that picture show?

answers.text: The enemy was few in number
The enemy was hard to see

cards.text: The enemy pursued them over the mountains and ambushed them in the wilderness.
Then the poet names another painful loss: the king, the LORD's anointed. He says, "The LORD’s anointed, the breath of our life, was captured in their pits."

cards.question: The people had high hopes for the LORD's anointed before he was captured. What had they said about him?

answers.text: They would live under his shadow
He would rebuild the temple walls
He would make them rich again

cards.text: Then the poet turns to Edom, the nation that came from Esau (Genesis 36:9). He says, "So rejoice and be glad, O Daughter of Edom, you who dwell in the land of Uz."

cards.question: Edom is rejoicing now. Yet the poet says the cup will pass to Edom as well. What does he say will happen when it does?

answers.text: She will get drunk and expose herself
She will share it with her allies
She will pour it out on the ground

cards.text: Then the poet speaks straight to the Daughter of Zion.

cards.question: The poet tells the Daughter of Zion that her punishment is complete.

cards.text: And the poet says the LORD will not prolong her exile. After a whole poem of dark, friend, that's good news.

cards.question: The poet says the LORD will let the iniquity of the Daughter of Edom go unpunished.
